He treated culture as the terrain on which colonised peoples first resisted, and insisted that no revolution could be victorious without the full participation of women.

Cabral was assassinated on 20 January 1973 in Conakry by disaffected PAIGC members, months before Guinea-Bissau's unilateral declaration of independence. His writings and organising method became foundational for Pan-Africanism, for African anti-colonial movements from Mozambique to South Africa, and for Black radicals in the Americas from Amiri Baraka to the members of the Black Panther Party. Within afro-anarchist reading he is a bridge between armed anti-colonial struggle and a serious materialist analysis of race, class and culture.

articles.title: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o was a Kenyan novelist, playwright, essayist and academic widely regarded as East Africa's leading novelist and one of the most influential voices in modern African literature. His fifty-year fight to write in Gikuyu rather than English put the question of language at the centre of decolonisation.
articles.body:
Born James Ngugi in 1938 in the small Kenyan town of Kamiriithu, he grew up amid the violence of the Mau Mau uprising and the British counter-insurgency — a childhood that returns again and again in his fiction. Weep Not, Child (1964) was the first English-language novel by an East African writer, followed by The River Between (1965) and A Grain of Wheat (1967), which reworks the mission-school Christianity he was raised in as a story of betrayal and communal loss.

Around 1970 he renounced his baptismal name and his 'colonialist' language, taking the name Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o and vowing to write his fiction and plays in Gikuyu. The turn was consolidated by the community theatre project at Kamiriithu, which produced Ngaahika Ndeenda ('I Will Marry When I Want'), co-written with Ngũgĩ wa Mirii, using peasants and workers as actors and audience.

The play, together with his novel Petals of Blood (1977), enraged the Kenyatta government, which detained him in Kamiti Maximum Security Prison in 1977–78 without trial. He used the time to write Caitani Mũtharaba-inĩ ('Devil on the Cross') on prison-issue toilet paper. On his release the regime blocked him from academic work, and he spent decades in exile — in the United Kingdom and then the United States, teaching at Yale, NYU and, for many years, UC Irvine.

His essay collection Decolonising the Mind (1986) argued that European languages carry European worldviews into African minds, and that African liberation is inseparable from African-language literature. Later novels — including the giant satire Wizard of the Crow (2006) — put that argument into fictional practice at epic scale.

Ngũgĩ died on 28 May 2025 in Buford, Georgia, at 87. His life pairs the discipline of the griot with the risks of the political prisoner, and he remains an anchor for any afro-anarchist library serious about the politics of language.

articles.title: Ashanti Alston
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Ashanti Omowali Alston is an anarchist activist, speaker and writer, a former member of the Black Panther Party and the Black Liberation Army, and one of the founders of Anarchist People of Color. His life traces a straight line from Black Power to Black anarchism.
articles.body:
Alston was born in 1954 in Plainfield, New Jersey. He was 11 years old when Malcolm X was assassinated and 13 when Newark rose in the 1967 riots — events that unfolded a short bus ride from his home and shaped his politics before he had a vocabulary for them. As a teenager he joined the Black Panther Party's youth wing and helped run breakfast and community programmes.

In 1971, in the wake of the Panther 21 trial in New York, he joined the underground Black Liberation Army. In 1974 he was arrested for a bank robbery carried out to fund the organisation and sentenced to prison, where he would spend the next eleven years.

Inside, Alston read voraciously: Marxism-Leninism, Maoism, guerrilla theory, and, decisively, the writings of anarchists smuggled in through Panther comrades. Anarchism gave him a way to name what had gone wrong inside the movements he loved — the way charismatic male leaders had come to substitute themselves for the collective, the way Marxist-Leninist parties recreated the coercive structures they were meant to smash. He came out of prison in 1985 already thinking of himself as a Black anarchist.

In the 1990s and 2000s he became one of the most listened-to voices in the emerging Black anarchist and anti-authoritarian scene in the United States. He co-founded Anarchist People of Color (APOC), spoke widely about the Black Panthers and the Zapatistas, and served on the Steering Committee of the Jericho Movement, which organises for US political prisoners. He was married to fellow BPP and BLA member Safiya Bukhari, herself a foundational figure in prisoner-support organising, until her death in 2003.

For an afro-anarchist library Alston is essential: his talks and essays — 'Black Anarchism', 'Beyond Nationalism But Not Without It', 'Anarcho-Pantherista' — are among the clearest bridges we have between the Black Liberation tradition and non-Eurocentric anarchist practice.

articles.title: Chale Wote Street Art Festival
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: The Chale Wote Street Art Festival is an annual alternative art festival in Accra, Ghana, organised by ACCRA [dot] ALT with Redd Kat Pictures and the Chale Wote Street Art Projekt. Since 2011 it has turned the streets of historic Jamestown into a continent-wide meeting place for street painting, film, spoken word, sound art and performance.
articles.body:
The festival's name comes from Ga, the language of the fishing communities of coastal Accra: chale wote means 'friend, let's go' and is also the local nickname for the plastic flip-flops most Ghanaians grow up in. It is a fitting name for a festival built on foot, in the street, by people who don't need permission from a gallery.

The first edition opened in Jamestown in 2011 with a single day of murals, graffiti, spoken word and performance along the seafront by the old British and Dutch trading forts. The organisers — chiefly Mantse Aryeequaye and Sionne Neely — deliberately chose one of Accra's oldest and most economically neglected neighbourhoods, insisting that contemporary African art belonged in the alleys and courtyards of ordinary people rather than the air-conditioned white cubes of Osu.

Each year the festival adopts a theme — 'Africa Electric', 'Spirit Robot', 'Pidgin Imaginarium', 'Para Other' — and runs a full week of programmes. Alongside the outdoor murals and installations there are film screenings, extreme sports demonstrations, fashion labs, sound performances, a kids' lab, and a procession of masking cultures drawn from Ga, Yoruba, Igbo and diaspora traditions. Artists and collectives arrive from across Africa and the Black Atlantic.

Over the years the festival has spread beyond Jamestown to venues including the Nubuke Foundation, the Museum of Science and Technology, and neighbourhoods like Nima and Osu, while keeping its base in the old town. It has helped build the careers of artists such as Serge Attukwei Clottey — whose 'Afrogallonism' work with recycled yellow jerrycans first found its audience in the streets of La — and Va-Bene Elikem Fiatsi.

For an afro-anarchist library Chale Wote is a live case study of a self-organised, anti-institutional cultural infrastructure: a festival that treats the street as commons, insists on free entry, and makes contemporary African art on the terms of the neighbourhood that hosts it.

articles.title: El Anatsui
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: El Anatsui is a Ghanaian sculptor, long based in Nsukka, Nigeria, whose vast metal tapestries — stitched from thousands of flattened liquor-bottle caps — are among the defining works of contemporary African art. He won the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale in 2015 and the Praemium Imperiale in 2017.
articles.body:
Born in 1944 in Anyako in Ghana's Volta Region, Anatsui trained at the College of Art in Kumasi in the 1960s, a period when the young Ghanaian state and its intellectuals were arguing hard about what an independent African modernism should look like. He rejected the school's imported European curriculum and began drawing on Ewe adinkra symbols, Uli wall painting from south-eastern Nigeria and the visual vocabulary of West African textiles.

In 1975 he moved to the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, becoming part of what came to be called the Nsukka School — a loose group of artists, including Uche Okeke and Obiora Udechukwu, committed to grounding contemporary Nigerian art in indigenous forms. He taught at Nsukka for four decades and became a full professor of sculpture in 1996.

His early work was in wood and ceramic, chainsawed and burned to speak of ruptures and healings in African history. Around 2000 he began collecting the aluminium caps and neck-wrappers discarded by a liquor recycling plant near his studio in Nsukka. Flattened and pierced with copper wire, they became the raw material of the huge, shimmering wall-hangings — Man's Cloth, Woman's Cloth, Dusasa, Gravity and Grace, Behind the Red Moon — that have travelled from the façade of the Palazzo Fortuny to Tate Modern's Turbine Hall.

Each hanging is deliberately loose: it has no fixed shape, and can be re-draped by every institution that receives it, so that no two installations are identical. The material carries the trace of the transatlantic drink trade — European spirits exchanged for African bodies — while the finished cloth answers back with a form drawn from kente, adire and other African textile traditions.

Anatsui has been included in almost every major biennale since the 1990s and was on Time's list of the hundred most influential people in 2023. For an afro-anarchist library he stands for a slow, teacher-in-a-university-town practice of contemporary African art: made from the discarded objects of empire, made with many hands, and made to be remade wherever it lands.

articles.title: Octavia E. Butler
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Octavia Estelle Butler (1947–2006) was an acclaimed American science fiction author who became the first sci-fi writer to receive a MacArthur Fellowship. Overcoming childhood shyness and dyslexia in Pasadena, she reshaped speculative fiction around power, hierarchy, survival, and the possibility of transformation through difference.
articles.body:
Butler's path from a shy, bullied child at the Pasadena Central Library to celebrated novelist ran through community college, temporary jobs, and the Clarion Workshop, which launched her professional career. By the late 1970s she was writing full-time, publishing the Patternist series and her breakthrough novel Kindred.

Kindred offered one of the first sustained treatments of an interracial marriage in twentieth-century American literature. It follows Dana, a Black woman repeatedly pulled from 1976 Los Angeles into an early nineteenth-century Maryland plantation, where she meets her enslaved ancestors. Through that temporal bridge, Butler examined how historical trauma continues to shape present identity and survival.

Parable of the Sower, published in 1993, is her mature dystopian vision. Set in a deteriorating 2020s California, it follows Lauren Olamina, a young woman with hyperempathy who develops the Earthseed philosophy — a religion premised on humanity's future among the stars. The novel prophetically addressed environmental collapse, economic inequality, and religious extremism, imagining communities built on diversity and mutual survival.

Its 1998 sequel, Parable of the Talents, deepens the story by depicting institutional violence against Earthseed and the endurance required to keep hope alive under systematic oppression. Both books have become touchstones for organizers, sci-fi writers, and Afrofuturist theorists who read them as blueprints for surviving late-capitalist collapse.

Butler's thematic preoccupations — hierarchical violence, genetic transformation, interspecies intimacy, and marginalized protagonists building alternative futures — placed her at the center of Afrofuturism, even as her insistence on multi-ethnic and cross-species hybridity complicated straightforward racial narratives. She consciously wrote herself in, centering Black women's perspectives typically excluded from speculative fiction.

Her legacy shaped a generation of writers of color exploring social justice through imagined futures. The 2015 anthology Octavia's Brood drew directly on her work, adaptations of Kindred and Parable of the Sower continue to appear as graphic novels and operas, and NASA named the Mars Perseverance rover's landing site in her honor.

articles.title: Nnedi Okorafor and the Rise of Africanfuturism
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Nnedimma Nkemdili Okorafor is a Nigerian American writer of science fiction and fantasy for both children and adults. Best known for the Binti trilogy and Who Fears Death, she has won the Hugo, Nebula, and World Fantasy Awards while coining the term Africanfuturism to describe her Africa-rooted speculative practice.
articles.body:
Okorafor coined Africanfuturism in 2019 to distinguish her literary approach from Afrofuturism as it had been theorized in the diaspora. Africanfuturism centers African settings, cultures, and cosmologies within speculative fiction, refusing to treat the continent as backdrop or destination for outsiders. The framework reflects her dual Nigerian and American heritage, producing stories that emerge from lived experience across both worlds.

The Binti trilogy, published between 2015 and 2018, exemplifies this vision. It follows a young Himba mathematician navigating intergalactic conflict as the first of her people to attend a distant space university. The first novella won both the 2015 Nebula and the 2016 Hugo, establishing Okorafor's prominence within speculative fiction's highest honors. The books blend hard science fiction with Igbo and Himba cultural elements, from otjize clay to mathematical harmonizing.

Who Fears Death (2010) was her adult breakthrough and won the World Fantasy Award for Best Novel. Set in a post-apocalyptic Sudan, it centers a mixed-race protagonist confronting genocide and environmental collapse, demonstrating Okorafor's commitment to placing Black girls in roles usually reserved for white male characters. HBO optioned it for television with George R.R. Martin executive producing.

Akata Witch (2011) and its sequels introduced contemporary Nigerian settings infused with magical realism and Nsibidi script symbolism. The series reached mainstream recognition when Akata Woman debuted on the New York Times bestseller list in 2022, validating her vision of African-centered fantasy for young readers.

Okorafor's influence extends well beyond her own bibliography. By insisting that publishers foreground African narratives, mythology, and futures rather than exoticize them, she reshaped genre conventions and opened commercial space for a generation of speculative writers on the continent and across the diaspora, from Tade Thompson to Suyi Davies Okungbowa.

articles.title: N. K. Jemisin: The Broken Earth and Three Consecutive Hugos
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Nora Keita Jemisin is an American science fiction and fantasy writer born in Iowa City in 1972. Her fiction explores cultural conflict and oppression through elaborate world-building, and she made history as the first author ever to win three consecutive Hugo Awards for Best Novel — one for each book in the Broken Earth trilogy.
articles.body:
Jemisin's breakthrough came with The Hundred Thousand Kingdoms (2010), the first book in her Inheritance trilogy, which won the Locus Award for Best First Novel. The trilogy, completed with The Broken Kingdoms and The Kingdom of Gods, established her as a distinctive voice in contemporary fantasy — one who took theological politics seriously and wrote women of color as protagonists without apology.

Her most celebrated work, the Broken Earth trilogy, began with The Fifth Season in 2015. She has said the story grew partly from a dream and partly from the Ferguson protests. The series unfolds on a geologically unstable supercontinent where a caste of people called orogenes can quiet or unleash earthquakes, and are enslaved for their gift. It is a searing allegory of racialized violence, ecological collapse, and generational trauma.

Between 2016 and 2018 The Fifth Season, The Obelisk Gate, and The Stone Sky each won the Hugo Award for Best Novel in successive years. Jemisin thus became the first African American writer to win the Hugo for Best Novel and the first author ever to sweep three consecutive Hugos for a single trilogy.

Her work has become a lodestar for readers and critics rethinking what speculative fiction can be. By centering marginalized perspectives and interrogating power structures, she has helped reshape both the demographics and the aesthetics of the field.

Jemisin received the MacArthur Fellowship in 2020 and was named the SFWA Grand Master in 2025, cementing her legacy alongside Butler, Delany, and Le Guin as a defining figure of twenty-first century speculative literature.

articles.title: Space Is the Place: Sun Ra's Afrofuturist Manifesto
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Space Is the Place is an Afrofuturist science fiction film released in 1974, directed by John Coney and written by Sun Ra and Joshua Smith. Sun Ra and his Arkestra star in a fragmented, blaxploitation-inflected fable in which the composer returns from outer space to recruit African Americans to a new planet.
articles.body:
The narrative follows Sun Ra's return from outer space with his crew to recruit African Americans for settlement on a newly discovered planet. Using music as his mode of transportation, Ra travels back to 1943 Chicago, where he plays the Overseer — a pimp-overlord figure — in a high-stakes card game whose stakes are the fate of the Black race.

In the early 1970s he lands in Oakland to establish an Outer Space Employment Agency, recruiting local youth while navigating suspicion and interference from community members and NASA scientists alike. The film's plot dissolves into ritual: recruitment as ritual, music as ritual, escape as ritual.

The production emerged from Dilexi, an experimental art series produced by Jim Newman and directed by John Coney. It was deliberately fragmented: Seth Hill captured Arkestra performance footage, and Joshua Smith helped stitch the disparate elements together with a loose blaxploitation-inflected story. Editor Barbara Pokras resolved what one critic called the film's death-defying existential leaps in continuity.

Scholars have read the film as Sun Ra's performative response to the Black Panther Party — a counter-proposal in which the band's use of technology and music, rather than terrestrial armed struggle, will liberate the people by changing consciousness. Sun Ra himself insisted the myth was the mechanism.

Two cuts exist: the abridged 64-minute Sun Ra edit that circulated on VHS for decades, and the uncut 82-minute version released through Plexifilm in 2003, with both versions reissued by Harte Recordings in 2015. The film has become required viewing for anyone tracing Afrofuturism's cinematic lineage, from The Brother from Another Planet to Neptune Frost.

articles.title: Pumzi: Wanuri Kahiu's Kenyan Sci-Fi Short
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Pumzi is a Kenyan science fiction short film written and directed by Wanuri Kahiu that premiered at the 2010 Sundance Film Festival. The 21-minute work — whose Swahili title means breath — explores environmental collapse and human resilience through the eyes of a woman quietly refusing her community's authoritarian consensus.
articles.body:
Set thirty-five years after the Water War, Pumzi unfolds inside the Maitu community, an isolated underground refuge where survivors have adapted to extreme scarcity. The protagonist Asha works as curator of a Virtual Natural History Museum and discovers a mysterious soil sample containing moisture and no radiation. When she inhales its scent, she experiences a vision of a lush tree and water, challenging the founding belief that life outside is impossible.

Her attempt to share the evidence with the governing three-woman Council proves futile. They dismiss her findings as delusions, confiscate her discovery, and reassign her to manual labor generating electricity on human-powered treadmills. The society's ingenious recycling of water and sweat masks a suffocating authoritarian control over movement and thought.

Asha escapes with help from a bathroom attendant — the film's most tender human connection, achieved entirely without dialogue. She traverses a devastated landscape littered with plastic waste, following navigational instincts toward the soil sample's origin. Rather than a thriving ecosystem, she finds a desert.

In a final act of regenerative hope she plants a seedling using her last water and the moisture of her own body. The concluding image of her prostrate form transforming into vegetation reverses the film's opening composition, offering ecological restoration through personal sacrifice.

The work stands as foundational Africanfuturist cinema. Kahiu has said the high price of bottled water partly inspired the project's focus on scarcity. Pumzi examines how technological efficiency can enable surveillance, how mediation erodes authentic communication, and how individual courage can crack institutional certainty. It also opened the international festival circuit to a new generation of Kenyan and East African speculative filmmakers.

articles.title: Neptune Frost: A Coltan-Miner Cyber Musical
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Neptune Frost is a 2021 science fiction musical co-directed by Saul Williams and Anisia Uzeyman. Set in a fictional post-civil-war Burundi, it follows an intersex hacker and a coltan miner whose union leads a fugitive collective in a revolt against global tech extraction. It premiered at Cannes to wide acclaim.
articles.body:
Williams originally conceived the project as a graphic novel in 2013, developed it as a stage musical, and then adapted it for film. His 2016 album MartyrLoserKing supplied much of the thematic material. A 2018 Kickstarter campaign, with Lin-Manuel Miranda as executive producer, helped fund production, and Ezra Miller joined as producer in 2020. The film was shot over 27 days in Rwanda, marking the directorial debut for both Williams and Rwandan cinematographer Anisia Uzeyman.

The narrative centers on Neptune, an intersex runaway, and Matalusa, a coltan miner working under lethal conditions. His brother Tekno's death in the mines catalyzes Matalusa's flight; Neptune's grief at their aunt's funeral mirrors that loss. Visions of their unborn child pull the two together, and they found Unanimous Goldmine, a hacker village challenging corporate control of the internet.

Neptune's technokinetic abilities enable the collective to broadcast a liberatory signal globally, until state discovery brings the destruction of the village. The film insists on the entanglement of extractive mining, undersea cables, queer refusal, and diasporic ancestor communion.

It screened at Cannes Directors' Fortnight, Toronto, the New York Film Festival, and Sundance before its June 2022 U.S. limited release through Kino Lorber. It won the Melbourne International Film Festival's inaugural Bright Horizons award of A$140,000, honoring ambitious independent filmmaking on social justice themes.

Critical reception was rapturous. Rotten Tomatoes reported 96 percent positive reviews, with critics calling it bursting with ideas and ambition, and Metacritic scored it 83 out of 100 for universal acclaim. It received an Independent Spirit Award nomination for Best Cinematography, acknowledging Uzeyman's visionary contribution to a work that reroutes the coltan supply chain into a queer Pan-African epic.

articles.title: Julie Dash and Daughters of the Dust
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Julie Ethel Dash is an American filmmaker, music video director, and author. Her groundbreaking 1991 feature Daughters of the Dust is the first full-length film directed by an African American woman to receive wide theatrical distribution in the United States, and its Gullah-Geechee imagery continues to shape Black visual culture.
articles.body:
Dash was among the pioneering cohort of Black filmmakers at UCLA who came to be known as the LA Rebellion. These artists worked to overturn Hollywood's prejudicial portrayals by making experimental narratives centered on authentic African American life. Her 1982 short Illusions, which addresses racial and sexual passing in wartime Hollywood, later received preservation status in the National Film Registry.

Drawing on her father's Gullah heritage, Dash developed Daughters of the Dust over many years before its Sundance premiere in 1991. The film centers three generations of Gullah women on St. Helena Island in 1902 as they prepare to migrate north. It employs the island's authentic Creole dialect with minimal subtitles, refusing translation as an act of cultural sovereignty.

The film's structure is deliberately non-linear, mirroring the storytelling of West African griots and honoring the ways Black women pass down both talent and secrets across generations. A Gullah consultant guided the production, and Arthur Jafa's cinematography lent it the slow, saturated stillness that would define an entire strand of Black art cinema to come.

Daughters of the Dust entered the National Film Registry in 2004 and continues to expand its influence. Beyoncé cited it explicitly as a visual template for Lemonade in 2016, particularly the women in white on the beach — an image that traveled back into pop culture at scale.

Dash's practice belongs to Afrofuturism read broadly: a cinema of ancestral time, of Black interior worlds, of a past that refuses to stay past. Her work rewired what a Black American film could look like and made room for filmmakers from Ava DuVernay to Garrett Bradley to Numa Perrier.

articles.title: The Sun Ra Arkestra: A Cosmic Ensemble Across Seven Decades
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: The Sun Ra Arkestra is an American jazz ensemble formed in the mid-1950s under keyboardist and composer Sun Ra's direction until his 1993 death. Considered pioneers of Afrofuturism, the group has been led by saxophonist Marshall Allen since 1995 and still performs, capes and headdresses intact.
articles.body:
The ensemble emerged in Philadelphia during the 1950s as Sun Ra's working band, later making its home in a Germantown rowhouse that has served as the group's creative center ever since. The Arkestra draws from swing, rock and roll, Chicago blues, free improvisation, and early electronic instruments, producing a sound that refuses categorization within jazz alone.

A pivotal moment arrived in 1968 when vocalist June Tyson joined. Tyson's contribution extended beyond her singing and spoken word into costume design and choreography, and she worked closely with Sun Ra until her death in 1992. She helped establish the visual language — Afrofuturist regalia dominated by colorful capes and headdresses — that became iconic.

When Sun Ra passed in 1993, saxophonist John Gilmore briefly assumed leadership before Marshall Allen took the helm in 1995. Allen, a member since 1958, has stewarded the group across the intervening decades with quiet integrity. Under his direction the Arkestra released A Song for the Sun in 1999, their first original studio album as a collective without Sun Ra.

Sun Ra's cosmic philosophy — that Black people would find their liberation not on this planet but in the outer spaces of myth, sound, and disciplined creative practice — remains the group's animating logic. It positions them not as entertainers but as itinerant priests of a working Afrofuturist religion.

Allen's stewardship has proven remarkably durable, and he has led the group past his own 100th birthday. Recent achievements include a 2026 Grammy nomination for Lights on a Satellite in the Best Large Jazz Ensemble Album category, affirming that the Arkestra's philosophical coherence and musical urgency have both crossed the century mark.

articles.title: Janelle Monáe: Cindi Mayweather and the ArchAndroid
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Janelle Monáe Robinson is an American singer, songwriter, rapper, and actor born in Kansas City in 1985. Across a decade of concept albums, films, and androgynous tuxedos, she has built one of the most sustained Afrofuturist projects in contemporary pop.
articles.body:
Monáe developed an android alter ego, Cindi Mayweather, to explore otherness and marginalization from within the science fiction canon. She has said the android represents the new other, allowing listeners who feel excluded to identify with her narrative. The Metropolis suite, beginning with her 2007 EP, presents Cindi as a fugitive android who fell in love with a human and is hunted for the transgression. Fritz Lang's 1927 Metropolis is her declared godfather text.

Her 2010 debut album The ArchAndroid extended the Metropolis narrative, positioning Cindi as a messianic figure liberating the android community from oppressive forces. Monáe used the mythology to examine contemporary treatment of marginalized communities, framing her android as the mediator between the mind and the hand, and between oppressor and oppressed.

Released in 2018, Dirty Computer stepped away from explicit sci-fi framing while keeping the conceptual ambition. It received Album of the Year nomination at the 61st Grammys and was accompanied by a science fiction emotion-picture companion, extending her long-running commitment to multimedia storytelling and queer futurity.

Monáe moved into acting with roles in Moonlight and Hidden Figures in 2016, where she played engineer Mary Jackson, then Harriet in 2019 and Glass Onion in 2022, where she earned wide acclaim for a dual performance. The acting career has complemented her music, and both have circled the same set of questions about who gets to belong to the future.

Her body of work sits at the intersection of Afrofuturism, queer theory, and Southern Black soul lineage, and has shaped how younger artists from FKA Twigs to Yves Tumor approach genre as costume.

articles.title: Moor Mother and Black Quantum Futurism
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Camae Ayewa, who records as Moor Mother, is an American poet, musician, and activist based in Philadelphia. Since 2012 she has emerged as one of the most distinctive voices in experimental music, integrating poetry, sound, and organizing work across a growing body of solo and collective projects.
articles.body:
Ayewa's practice bridges poetry and experimental music with a deliberate political intention. She studied photography at Philadelphia's Art Institute before establishing herself as a multidisciplinary creator whose work interrogates historical narratives and material systems. Her 2016 debut Fetish Bones arrived with a 122-page book of poetry attached and drew serious attention from Pitchfork, Rolling Stone, and The Wire.

As one half of Black Quantum Futurism with Rasheedah Phillips, Ayewa develops speculative frameworks that center Black futures and refigure inherited notions of linear time. The collective's zines, sound works, and Community Futures Lab in North Philadelphia read as some of the most rigorous applied Afrofuturist practice anywhere.

Ayewa co-leads Irreversible Entanglements, a liberation-oriented free-jazz collective that emerged through Philadelphia's musical and activist communities. The ensemble surrounds her vocals and lyrics with muscular instrumental improvisation drawn from the Art Ensemble of Chicago's lineage.

Her solo albums — Analog Fluids of Sonic Black Holes in 2019, Circuit City in 2020, and Black Encyclopedia of the Air in 2021 — show an evolving engagement with sound design, performance art, and conceptual framework. They root Afrofuturist discourse in the material conditions of gentrified Black neighborhoods, prison abolition, and archival recovery.

Since 2021 Ayewa has served as an assistant professor at USC's Thornton School of Music, extending her influence into formal educational contexts while keeping her collective and independent practice fully intact.

articles.title: Kehinde Wiley and the Rewriting of the Old Masters
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Kehinde Wiley is an American portrait painter based in New York, born in 1977. His naturalistic paintings insert Black subjects into the poses and framings of Old Master portraits, and his 2018 portrait of Barack Obama for the Smithsonian brought his practice to a global audience.
articles.body:
Wiley's method emerged during a residency at the Studio Museum in Harlem, where a discarded NYPD mugshot fundamentally altered his vision of portraiture. He began recruiting men from urban streets — particularly Harlem's 125th Street and South Central Los Angeles — inviting them to assume poses drawn from Renaissance masterworks. The strategy fuses modern source material with historic portrait traditions to make heroic images that address the status of young Black men in contemporary life.

His signature aesthetic pairs meticulously rendered figures with explosively decorative backgrounds drawing from Rococo, Islamic pattern, and West African textile. Rather than the sweeping estates of classical portraiture he places his subjects in ornate floral and patterned fields that carry the visual weight of nobility.

In October 2017 Wiley received the commission to paint Obama's official portrait for the Smithsonian. The finished work depicts the former president seated on an antique chair amid botanical references to his life — Chicago chrysanthemums, Kenyan lilies for his father, Hawaiian jasmine. After the February 2018 unveiling alongside Amy Sherald's portrait of Michelle Obama, National Portrait Gallery attendance nearly doubled from 1.1 to 2.1 million visitors.

Wiley's 2005 Rumors of War paintings reimagined equestrian portraiture with contemporary subjects in sportswear. Responding to the Confederate monuments on Richmond's Monument Avenue, he expanded the concept into a 30-foot bronze sculpture of a young Black man in jeans, Nike high-tops, and locs, unveiled in Times Square in 2019 and installed permanently at the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts.

His practice sits comfortably within the Afrofuturist lineage of Black artists who take control of representation as a first-order political act, and his Black Rock artist residency in Dakar has built a physical infrastructure for Black diasporic artistic exchange.

articles.title: Aïda Muluneh's Afrofuturist Photography
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Aïda Muluneh is an Ethiopian photographer and artist born in Addis Ababa in 1974, renowned for striking Afrofuturist portraits that fuse vivid body paint with cinematic staging. Her work and her institution-building have reshaped how contemporary African photography circulates internationally.
articles.body:
Muluneh's photographic practice centers the strategic use of body adornment as a primary medium. She approaches each image as a film production in which character, set, lighting, and styling assemble in a single frame, with face and body painting as the foundational technique. The work draws on traditional body ornamentation practices across cultures, carrying the past forward into an imagined future.

Her signature aesthetic uses saturated primary colors — deep reds, cobalt blues, saffron yellows — that reference Ethiopian church murals and cohere at architectural distance. These chromatic choices are both aesthetic and cultural, grounding contemporary work in historical and geographic specificity.

In 2010 Muluneh founded Addis Foto Fest, which has grown into Africa's largest photography festival and is held biennially in the Ethiopian capital. The festival democratizes photographic practice by bringing exhibitions, workshops, and portfolio reviews to broad audiences, and by building an international bridge for photographers on the continent.

Her work predominantly features female subjects, and she has spoken openly about her belief in the power in the gaze of a woman, noting that educating women creates cascading benefits across a society. That commitment translates into images where women stand as sovereign subjects rather than as ethnographic evidence.

Muluneh's artistic mission directly refuses what she has called Africa's damaging single story of poverty and despair, offering instead a visual language of complexity, dignity, and futurity. Her prints are held in collections including the Smithsonian's National Museum of African Art and have circulated through solo exhibitions from Addis Ababa to Paris.

articles.title: Ytasha Womack: Naming Afrofuturism for a New Generation
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Ytasha L. Womack is an American writer, filmmaker, and cultural critic recognized for her work on Afrofuturism, race, and speculative culture. She is best known for Afrofuturism: The World of Black Sci-Fi and Fantasy Culture (2013), which blends storytelling with scholarship to trace how Black culture builds and inhabits the future.
articles.body:
Womack's flagship book gave a wide public readership its first accessible introduction to Afrofuturism, framing it as a movement whose members range across music, literature, comics, fashion, and organizing. The volume assembles interviews, historical arcs, and personal narrative, and it earned a 2014 Locus Awards Non-Fiction Finalist nod, cementing its standing in both academic and creative circles.

As a scholar and cultural critic, Womack contributes to conversations about technology, race, and future possibility through multiple platforms — from public lectures and TED talks to workshops for young people. Her writing demonstrates how Black perspectives reshape speculative narrative rather than simply appearing within it.

She lectures at universities including DePaul and Rutgers, bringing Afrofuturist concepts into classrooms where they had not previously been legible as a discipline. Her second book, A Guide to Afrofuturism (2023), tightened that curriculum for a new wave of readers.

Womack's multifaceted approach — combining novels, dance-film work, journalism, and educational programs — positions her as a genuine node in the contemporary Afrofuturist ecosystem rather than only a commentator on it. Her scholarship insists that Afrofuturism is a critical framework for understanding culture, technology, and liberation, not a nostalgia project.

Her broader impact runs through a generation of scholars and artists who now cite her book as the entry point that gave them permission to name what they had been doing all along.

articles.title: AFROPUNK: From Documentary to Global Black Alternative Festival
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: The Afropunk Festival is a celebration of Black alternative music and culture that began in 2005 at the Brooklyn Academy of Music. Founded by James Spooner and Matthew Morgan, it grew out of Spooner's 2003 documentary on Black punk musicians and has since expanded across continents.
articles.body:
The festival's roots trace to Spooner's 2003 film Afro-Punk, which followed Black punk rock musicians across the United States. The documentary inspired the inaugural Brooklyn event in 2005, targeted specifically at Black alternative-minded punks and supported by the Brooklyn Academy of Music. It was small, unruly, and openly countercultural in a Black music landscape that then had little room for it.

Between 2009 and 2019, Jocelyn A. Cooper became instrumental in steering the festival's trajectory as it expanded to Atlanta, Paris, London, Johannesburg, Salvador, Miami, and Minneapolis. Performances by Erykah Badu, Tyler the Creator, and FKA Twigs elevated its prominence and helped establish an aesthetic — locs, chest tattoos, tulle, chainmail, custom denim — that traveled from the festival grounds into global fashion editorial.

Beyond music, Afropunk developed into a multifaceted platform. The 2020 virtual edition, Planet Afropunk: Past, Present, and Future is Black, featured virtual art galleries, Black hair showcases, and panels on systemic racism, prison reform, and the criminal justice system.

Following its acquisition by entrepreneur Richelieu Dennis and Essence Ventures, the festival continued to expand internationally, holding events in Brazil's Bahia region and multiple U.S. cities while facing ongoing debate from long-time attendees about whether corporate scale can coexist with the movement's original alternative ethos.

Afropunk sits in the wider Afrofuturist and Black alternative lineage as one of the few sustained physical infrastructures for it, a place where the futures gestured at in Sun Ra records and Octavia Butler novels take on flesh, sweat, and volume for a weekend at a time.

articles.title: Rosewater: Tade Thompson's Nigerian Alien Biodome
articles.author: Wikipedia contributors · ANARCHISM.AFRICA Editorial (summary)
articles.summary: Rosewater is a 2016 science fiction novel by Nigerian-British author Tade Thompson that reimagines the alien-invasion story through an African lens. Set across several decades in Nigeria, it explores psychic connection, technological integration, and humanity's negotiation with an unknowable extraterrestrial intelligence.
articles.body:
Thompson's debut follows Kaaro, a psychically gifted protagonist navigating a world transformed by Wormwood, an alien entity that arrives in London in 2012 and rearranges global geopolitics on impact. By the 2050s, Wormwood has raised an impenetrable dome over the Nigerian town of Rosewater and released xenoforms — fungal organisms that interface with human nervous systems and grant rare individuals, called sensitives, access to a collective information layer known as the xenosphere.

The narrative spans Kaaro's lifetime, beginning with his youth when he uses emerging telepathic abilities for theft before narrowly evading execution. He is later recruited by S45, a covert Nigerian government agency, and trained as an operative. His work involves tracking the anarchist revolutionary Oyin Da to the future site of Rosewater, where an encounter with Wormwood itself proves pivotal — he saves the alien from assassination and thereby helps trigger the raising of the protective dome.

In 2066 Kaaro confronts a crisis: sensitives are dying from unknown causes. His investigation reveals that Molara, an entity embodying the xenosphere itself, has begun systematically replacing human DNA with alien code across generations. His romantic entanglement with Aminat, unknowingly an S45 agent, sharpens the moral bind at the story's center.

Critics celebrated Thompson's genre mashup that fuses Africanfuturism, cyberpunk, and biopunk. Rosewater won the inaugural Nommo Award in 2017 and the Arthur C. Clarke Award in 2019, establishing Thompson as a leading contemporary Africanfuturist voice alongside Nnedi Okorafor and N.K. Jemisin.

By centering Nigeria rather than a Western capital, the novel refuses science fiction's default geography. It examines internet-era anxieties through the addictive connectivity of the xenosphere, critiques geopolitical isolationism, and confronts persistent social inequities including the criminalization of homosexuality. Rosewater launched the Wormwood Trilogy, completed by The Rosewater Insurrection and The Rosewater Redemption, both published in 2019, and earned a Hugo Best Series nomination in 2020.

events.title: Nyege Nyege Festival 2026
events.summary: East Africa's most vital underground music gathering returns to the banks of the Nile at Itanda Falls, Jinja. Four days of experimental, electronic, and traditional music from across the continent and diaspora — DJs, live acts, and sound systems operating without compromise.

events.title: Chale Wote Street Art Festival 2026
events.summary: Accra's annual free street art and performance festival transforms Jamestown — the oldest neighbourhood in the city — into an open-air gallery. Artists, performers, sound artists, and community members gather on the streets of the former fishing village for three days of collaborative public culture.

events.title: Sauti za Busara 2027
events.summary: The Swahili coast's premier music festival, held in the UNESCO-listed Stone Town of Zanzibar. Sauti za Busara (Sounds of Wisdom) brings together traditional and contemporary African musicians for four nights of outdoor performance at the Old Fort, with workshops, conversations, and daytime programming across the city.

events.title: Art X Lagos 2026
events.summary: Pan-African contemporary art fair bringing together galleries, artist-run spaces, and independent practitioners from across the continent and the diaspora. Now in its tenth year, Art X Lagos has established itself as the leading platform for African art in Africa — a market, a meeting point, and a space for rigorous public programming.

events.title: ROAPE Webinar: African Anarchisms
events.summary: The Review of African Political Economy's online discussion series turns its attention to anarchist and anti-authoritarian traditions in African political thought and practice. Scholars and organisers from across the continent and diaspora discuss the history of African anarchism, contemporary movements, and the relationship between anarchist theory and African liberation struggles.

events.title: Black to the Future — Afrofuturism Conference 2026
events.summary: A hybrid conference on Afrofuturism, technology, and Pan-African futures, held simultaneously in Cape Town and online. Speakers and artists from the continent and diaspora discuss speculative fiction, digital sovereignty, post-colonial technology, and the politics of imagining African futures beyond the frameworks of development and modernity.

events.title: Diaspora Rising: Afro-Anarchist Study Weekend
events.summary: A weekend of workshops, reading groups, and discussions on African anarchist praxis, organised with facilitators from the Zabalaza Anarchist Communist Front (ZACF), the Workers Solidarity Federation (WSF), and Black Rose/Rosa Negra. Open to all — sessions run in person in London and simultaneously online, with full recordings made available.

music.title: Zombie
music.summary: 12 minutes of horn-line indictment of the Nigerian military — the most-banned song of its decade.

music.title: Tezeta (Nostalgia)
music.summary: The defining piece of Ethio-jazz, from Mulatu of Ethiopia — vibraphone, tezeta scale, Addis at dusk.

music.title: Pata Pata
music.summary: Makeba's international anti-apartheid anthem — recorded in New York, banned at home.

music.title: Stimela (The Coal Train)
music.summary: Nine minutes on the migrant labour trains pulling Africa's miners into apartheid mines.

music.title: Africa Unite
music.summary: From Survival — Marley's pan-African call, recorded the year before the Zimbabwe independence concert.

music.title: My Queen Is Harriet Tubman
music.summary: From Your Queen Is a Reptile — tenor sax, two drum kits, tuba, no compromise.

music.title: Monsters You Made
music.summary: Lagos Afro-fusion broadside on the violence the post-colonial state inherits from its colonisers.

music.title: Mississippi Goddam
music.summary: Written after the murder of Medgar Evers and the bombing of Birmingham — a show-tune turned indictment.

music.title: The Revolution Will Not Be Televised
music.summary: Scott-Heron's spoken-word salvo against media co-optation — congas, flute, no studio polish.

music.title: Fire on the Mountain
music.summary: From Lagos via Paris — a quiet warning about the soldiers waiting for orders.

books.title: The Wretched of the Earth
books.author: Frantz Fanon
books.summary: Fanon's last work — colonialism, decolonial violence, and the psychology of liberation. Preface by Jean-Paul Sartre.
books.body:
Written in 1961 while Fanon was dying of leukaemia in a Soviet hospital in Moscow, The Wretched of the Earth is the most incendiary document to emerge from the era of Third World national liberation. Composed in ten weeks at Blida-Joinville psychiatric hospital in Algeria, where Fanon worked as a doctor and covertly assisted the FLN, the book is at once a political analysis and a clinical case study. Fanon did not theorise colonialism from the outside — he treated its casualties from within.

The book's opening chapter, On Violence, remains its most contested. Fanon argues that colonial violence is total — it occupies not just land and labour but the body and the psyche of the colonised — and that decolonisation necessarily involves a counter-violence that reorganises the colonised subject's sense of self. This is not a celebration of killing; it is a phenomenological account of what oppression does to human beings and what it costs to undo it. Jean-Paul Sartre's preface, which extended and sharpened this argument, became as controversial as the book itself.

The book's middle chapters on the pitfalls of national consciousness are prophetic. Fanon warned that if decolonisation merely transferred state power to a nationalist bourgeoisie that mimicked the colonial structure, it would reproduce exploitation under a Black flag. He described this class with forensic precision forty years before structural adjustment and privatisation made his diagnosis the common sense of the African left. The psychiatric chapters, drawn from Fanon's own clinical work, document the psychopathologies generated by colonial occupation — case studies that hold up as clinical literature and as political testimony simultaneously.

The Wretched of the Earth was banned by the French government on publication and has never been out of print. It was the handbook of the Black Panthers, the ANC underground, the Palestinian liberation movement, and every subsequent generation of anti-colonial thinkers. Achille Mbembe, bell hooks, and Judith Butler have all named it formative. It ends not with certainty but with a demand: that the Third World start over, invent something new, not imitate Europe.

books.title: How Europe Underdeveloped Africa
books.author: Walter Rodney
books.summary: The structural argument for African underdevelopment as a product of European capitalism — Rodney's defining work.
books.body:
Walter Rodney wrote How Europe Underdeveloped Africa in 1972 while teaching history at the University of Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, a city that had become the intellectual capital of the Pan-African liberation movement. The book was published simultaneously by Bogle-L'Ouverture in London and Tanzania Publishing House in Dar es Salaam — both radical, Africa-rooted operations — and immediately became the foundational text for understanding what colonialism had actually done to Africa economically.

Rodney's central argument is deceptively simple: underdevelopment is not a natural condition or a stage through which all societies pass. It is a relationship. African societies had development trajectories of their own before European contact; the slave trade and colonial extraction did not merely slow African development but actively redirected it, siphoning surplus wealth into European industrialisation. This is the dependency theory applied to Africa with meticulous historical documentation: trade statistics, land seizure records, wage data, crop yields, colonial budget allocations.

The book covers the full arc from pre-colonial African societies — which Rodney describes with careful attention to their sophistication and internal diversity — through the Atlantic slave trade, to colonialism proper and its economic mechanisms. He documents how colonial tax systems forced African peasants into wage labour; how cash-crop monocultures dismantled food sovereignty; how colonial education systems produced clerks rather than engineers. The argument is not that Africa was static before Europe arrived, but that Europe broke what was already moving.

Rodney was deported from Jamaica after teaching there and assassinated in Georgetown, Guyana in 1980 — a car bomb planted by agents of the Burnham government in which the CIA's involvement has never been definitively disproven. He was 38 years old. The book remains in print, has been translated into dozens of languages, and is taught in universities across Africa, the Caribbean, and the diaspora. A 2018 edition published by Verso with a new introduction by Angela Davis introduced it to another generation.

books.title: African Anarchism: The History of a Movement
books.author: Sam Mbah & I.E. Igariwey
books.summary: Written from Lagos — the reference text for African anarchist tradition, from acephalous societies through to contemporary movements.
books.body:
Sam Mbah and I.E. Igariwey wrote African Anarchism from Lagos in the mid-1990s, at a moment when Nigeria was under the military dictatorship of Sani Abacha and the possibility of stateless, self-organised social life felt both urgent and distant. Their central argument is one of the most generative in the literature: that pre-colonial African societies, particularly the many acephalous (stateless) societies organised around kinship, consensus decision-making, and communal land tenure, were not pre-political but were in fact functioning prefigurations of what anarchists elsewhere call mutual aid and horizontal organisation.

The book moves through several registers. It offers a historical survey of the diverse political structures of pre-colonial Africa, with particular attention to societies that managed complex economic and social life without the centralised authority of a state. It then traces the impact of colonialism on these structures — both the direct destruction of stateless societies by colonial administration, which required recognisable hierarchies to operate, and the ideological work of colonial ethnography in misrepresenting communal societies as primitive rather than functional. The third section, the most explicitly political, examines contemporary movements and argues for anarchism as the appropriate framework for African liberation.

Mbah and Igariwey are careful to distinguish their argument from romanticisation. They do not claim pre-colonial Africa was without conflict or exploitation. What they argue is that the dominant political forms — the institutions most people lived within most of the time — were organised along lines that anarchist theory independently arrived at through European working-class experience. The convergence is not coincidental; it reflects common human responses to the problem of organising collective life without hierarchy.

The book has been available as a free PDF on The Anarchist Library since its publication and remains one of the most downloaded texts there. It is the indispensable starting point for anyone working on African anarchism and is available in several languages. The Zabalaza Anarchist Communist Front in South Africa has long used it as a key organisational reference.

books.title: The Black Jacobins
books.author: C.L.R. James
books.summary: The history of the Haitian Revolution — Toussaint L'Ouverture, San Domingo, the only successful slave revolt in modern history.
books.body:
C.L.R. James published The Black Jacobins in 1938, the same year as his study of cricket and imperialism, Beyond a Boundary, and the year before he arrived in the United States where he would spend the next fifteen years writing and organising. The book is the definitive history of the Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1803 — the only successful slave revolt in the history of the modern world — and it is also something rarer: a work of history in which the enslaved are the protagonists, the strategists, the makers of their own liberation.

James centres Toussaint L'Ouverture not as a symbol but as a revolutionary tactician of the first order. He traces Toussaint's rise from enslaved coachman to general commanding the army that defeated Napoleon's expedition, the complex alliances he navigated with Spain, Britain, and France, and the contradictions that ultimately led to his capture and death in a French prison. James writes with the double consciousness of a Trinidadian Marxist who understands that Black history cannot be told through the frameworks built to exclude it — and so he builds a new one, drawing on Michelet and Marx simultaneously.

The book's title is deliberate. The Haitian revolutionaries were not imitating the French Jacobins — they were outrunning them. The enslaved people of San Domingo, who produced forty percent of Europe's sugar and fifty percent of its coffee, were the most exploited labour force in the Atlantic economy. Their uprising, which began in August 1791, defeated the armies of three European empires and produced the first free Black republic in the world in 1804. James argues that this was not a peripheral event in the history of modernity but one of its central chapters.

The Black Jacobins was revised and expanded in 1963 with a new appendix, From Toussaint L'Ouverture to Fidel Castro, drawing the line from the Haitian Revolution to Caribbean independence and African liberation. It remains in print, is taught in universities across the world, and is the indispensable text for understanding what Black self-emancipation looked like when it was total.

books.title: Decolonising the Mind
books.author: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o
books.summary: Why Ngũgĩ stopped writing in English. The politics of language as the politics of mind.
books.body:
Decolonising the Mind collects four essays on the politics of language in African literature, published in 1986 by James Currey and Heinemann — and simultaneously declared by Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o to be his farewell to the English language as a literary medium. He had been writing in Gikuyu since the late 1970s, a decision taken deliberately and at cost: his novel Petals of Blood was published in Gikuyu in 1977, the same year he was detained without charge by the Kenyan government under Daniel arap Moi for a year. This book explains why.

Ngũgĩ's core argument is that language is not merely a tool for communication but the medium through which a people perceive and name the world. Colonial conquest operated through language as surely as it operated through the gun: renaming the landscape, the people, the history; making the coloniser's tongue the language of education, law, literature, and aspiration; and in doing so, installing the coloniser's framework of reality inside the minds of the colonised. To write in English, Ngũgĩ argues, is to accept this framing — to address an imagined metropolitan reader rather than the African community whose life the literature supposedly represents.

The essays examine the oral literature tradition that colonial education systematically devalued; the language debate among African writers at the 1962 Makerere conference, where the question of English as medium was raised and largely sidestepped; and the specific experience of African-language education being displaced by European-language instruction, which Ngũgĩ documents through his own schooling in colonial Kenya. The prose is lucid and carries the weight of personal testimony — this is not abstract theorising but the account of a writer working through a decision that cost him his language community and ultimately his country.

Ngũgĩ was forced into exile in 1982 and did not return to Kenya permanently until 2004. Decolonising the Mind has been a central text in postcolonial studies, African literature curricula, and language-rights movements across the continent. It speaks directly to questions that are still unsettled: which languages African children are educated in, which languages receive state support, and whose voice gets to name the world.

books.title: Discourse on Colonialism
books.author: Aimé Césaire
books.summary: Césaire's foundational anti-colonial pamphlet — the boomerang of colonial violence returning to Europe as fascism.
books.body:
Aimé Césaire published Discours sur le colonialisme in French in 1950, the first English translation appeared in 1972 under the Monthly Review Press imprint, and the edition most widely read today — translated by Joan Pinkham and including a lengthy interview with René Depestre — was published in 2000. It is one of the most concentrated and rhetorically devastating pieces of anti-colonial writing in any language, composed in under a hundred pages with the precision of a surgical instrument.

The central move of the Discourse is what Césaire calls the boomerang effect: the argument that the barbarism that Europeans attributed exclusively to Africa and Asia was in fact the method Europe had perfected in its colonies, and that what returned to Europe as Nazism and fascism was not an aberration but a homecoming. Hitler did not invent the concentration camp — the British had camps in South Africa during the Boer War; the Germans had extermination campaigns in Namibia in 1904. What distinguished Nazism, in Césaire's reading, was not its method but its target: it applied to white Europeans what had previously been applied exclusively to non-Europeans. Europe's outrage was not about the violence but about the reversal of the racial order.

Césaire systematically demolishes the civilising mission — the claim that colonialism brought progress, Christianity, hygiene, and civilisation to primitive peoples. He documents what colonialism actually produced: the depopulation of Madagascar, the destruction of Congolese labour, the physical and cultural annihilation of communities across four continents. Against the colonial humanists who claimed to speak for the colonised, he insists on the right of the colonised to speak for themselves.

The text is also a statement of Négritude — the literary and intellectual movement Césaire co-founded with Léopold Sédar Senghor and Léon-Gontran Damas — and its vision of Black consciousness as a source of energy, not shame. The Discourse ends with a vision that will not compromise: not integration into European humanism but the construction of something new, a universal built from particulars that Europe has so far refused to acknowledge. It remains required reading in postcolonial studies and Black radical thought.

books.title: Black Marxism: The Making of the Black Radical Tradition
books.author: Cedric J. Robinson
books.summary: Robinson's case for racial capitalism, and for a Black radical tradition older than Marxism.
books.body:
Cedric J. Robinson published Black Marxism: The Making of the Black Radical Tradition in 1983, and it was largely ignored for the first two decades of its existence. It was reissued by the University of North Carolina Press in 2000, and the subsequent decades turned it into one of the most debated books in Black studies, sociology, and political theory. The concept it coined — racial capitalism — has since become indispensable to contemporary left analysis.

Robinson's argument has two interlocked parts. The first is a revisionist account of the origins of capitalism: he argues that racism does not emerge from capitalism as its product or instrument, as orthodox Marxism would have it, but predates it, rooted in the racial divisions of feudal Europe — the othering of Slavs, Irish, Jews, and other groups within European society before the Atlantic system was constructed. Capitalism was therefore always already racial; it could not have taken the form it took without the prior existence of racial hierarchy as a mechanism for organising labour and justifying exploitation. This is racial capitalism.

The second part traces what Robinson calls the Black radical tradition — the intellectual and political lineage running from the communities of enslaved Africans who refused the terms of their captivity through to W.E.B. Du Bois, C.L.R. James, and Richard Wright. Robinson's argument is that this tradition is not a subset of Marxism or of European radical thought but its own independent intellectual lineage, shaped by African social philosophies and the specific experience of racial capitalism. Du Bois, James, and Wright each arrived at Marxism and each eventually found it insufficient — not because they moved to the right but because they recognised that the Black experience of capitalism did not fit the frameworks built from white European working-class experience.

Black Marxism is a long, demanding, extensively documented book. It rewards the investment. The concept of racial capitalism has reshaped how activists, academics, and organisers understand the relationship between race and economic exploitation — and the argument for a Black radical tradition that cannot be subsumed into European frameworks has shaped Black studies, anarchist theory, and abolitionist politics across the world.

books.title: Sister Outsider
books.author: Audre Lorde
books.summary: Fifteen essays and speeches from Lorde — Black, lesbian, mother, warrior, poet — on intersectional refusal.
books.body:
Sister Outsider collects fifteen essays and speeches by Audre Lorde, published by Crossing Press in 1984. It is not a systematic work of political theory — it is something more difficult and more useful: a set of arguments made from the inside of a life, thinking through the politics of difference from the position of someone who embodied multiple forms of marginalisation simultaneously and refused to choose between them. Lorde identified herself throughout her life as a Black lesbian feminist socialist mother warrior poet, insisting on the whole phrase, refusing the reduction.

The collection includes some of the most important short texts in Black feminist writing. The Master's Tools Will Never Dismantle the Master's House, delivered as a keynote at the 1979 Second Sex Conference in New York, remains one of the most concise and devastating critiques of the white feminist establishment — Lorde's argument that the categories white feminism built its analysis around reproduced the same exclusions as the patriarchal structure it claimed to oppose. Poetry Is Not a Luxury makes the case that poetry is not decoration but a primary mode of knowledge, particularly for those whose access to official systems of knowledge has been systematically constrained. Uses of the Erotic reclaims the erotic from reduction to sexuality, arguing for it as a source of power and as a measure of what it feels like to be fully alive.

The essays on race, class, and age — particularly Age, Race, Class and Sex: Women Redefining Difference — anticipate what Kimberlé Crenshaw would later systematise as intersectionality theory. Lorde's approach is less taxonomic and more phenomenological: she is not cataloguing oppressions but describing what it feels like to live at their intersection, and arguing that the failure of progressive movements to engage with that experience costs them their potential.

Sister Outsider has been in continuous print for four decades and has influenced Black feminist theory, queer theory, anarchist thought, and abolitionist practice in equal measure. It is one of the books that teaches people how to think differently — not just what to think — and that is a rarer achievement than it sounds.

books.title: Are Prisons Obsolete?
books.author: Angela Y. Davis
books.summary: Davis's introductory case for prison abolition — short, urgent, foundational.
books.body:
Angela Y. Davis published Are Prisons Obsolete? in 2003 with Seven Stories Press, and at 128 pages it remains the most accessible entry point into prison abolition as a political project. Davis had been thinking about prisons since her own incarceration in 1970, when she was held in New York's Women's House of Detention on charges — ultimately dropped — connected to a courthouse shooting. By 2003, she had spent three decades studying the carceral system, and this short book distils that work into an argument anyone can follow.

The book's central argument is historical: that the prison is not a neutral institution for managing dangerous individuals but a successor to other systems of racialised social control. Davis traces the line from slavery to the convict leasing system — in which states leased incarcerated people to private businesses after the Civil War, functionally recreating slavery under a different name — to the twentieth-century prison-industrial complex. Mass incarceration in the United States, she argues, is not primarily about crime; it is primarily about managing a surplus Black and brown population excluded from formal labour markets, using a system whose racial proportions are not incidental but structural.

Davis argues against reform on the grounds that reforming the prison system tends to make prisons more manageable and therefore more durable — each improvement extends their legitimacy rather than questioning their existence. Abolition is not presented as a utopian demand but as a practical orientation: the question is not whether to abolish prisons immediately but to begin building the social institutions — mental health care, substance treatment, conflict resolution, economic security — that would make mass incarceration unnecessary. The book ends not with a blueprint but with a direction.

Are Prisons Obsolete? remains one of the most influential texts in the prison abolition movement worldwide. Its arguments have shaped the Movement for Black Lives platform, informed international debates about carceral reform, and provided the foundational vocabulary for a generation of organisers for whom abolition is not a slogan but a political horizon.

books.title: Necropolitics
books.author: Achille Mbembe
books.summary: The book-length expansion of the 2003 essay — sovereignty as the power to dictate who lives and who dies.
books.body:
Achille Mbembe first published Necropolitics as an essay in the journal Public Culture in 2003, translated from French by Libby Meintjes. It extended Michel Foucault's concept of biopower — the state's management of living populations — into territory Foucault had not visited: the colonial present, where sovereignty is expressed not as the management of life but as the prerogative to determine who must die. Mbembe called this necropower, and the expanded book published by Duke University Press in 2019 places this concept within his broader body of work on postcolonial subjectivity and the politics of enmity.

The essay and the book are inseparable from their historical occasions. Mbembe is writing from South Africa, thinking about Palestine, looking at the history of Atlantic slavery and apartheid — situations in which entire populations have been placed under what he calls death-worlds: social arrangements in which vast groups of people are subjected to conditions of life that approximate social and literal death. The slave ship is Mbembe's originating figure: a floating space of absolute violence, social death, and racial capitalism operating at its purest.

The analysis of occupation — particularly Israeli military occupation of Palestinian territories — is among the most precise and politically useful in the book. Mbembe describes the architecture of contemporary occupation: the carving of territory into cells, the control of movement, the destruction of infrastructure, the management of populations through the calibrated threat of lethal violence. This is sovereignty operating through the production of bare life, to use Agamben's term that Mbembe extends and complicates — but Mbembe insists, against Agamben, on the specifically colonial and racial character of this power.

Necropolitics has become a standard reference in postcolonial studies, critical theory, Black studies, and Palestinian solidarity discourse. The 2019 expanded edition adds chapters that situate necropower within Mbembe's developing argument about the Afropolitanism and the contemporary politics of difference. It is demanding reading but rewards the difficulty, particularly for anyone working on the relationship between colonial history and contemporary forms of state violence.

books.title: Pan-African Social Ecology: Speeches, Conversations, and Essays
books.author: Modibo Kadalie
books.publisher: Daraja Press / On Our Own Authority!
books.summary: Kadalie on autonomous mass democracy and African ecological traditions — interviews with Andrew Zonneveld.
books.body:
Pan-African Social Ecology collects speeches, conversations, and essays by Modibo Kadalie, a Black American organiser based in Atlanta whose thought synthesises Pan-Africanism, Murray Bookchin's social ecology, and the autonomous mass-democratic traditions of African communities. Published in 2019 by Daraja Press, the Ottawa-based decolonial publisher, and edited with Andrew Zonneveld, the collection represents decades of political thought developed through practice rather than academia.

Kadalie's central concern is the relationship between African land ethics and ecological politics. He argues that the communal land management traditions of pre-colonial African societies — traditions of collective stewardship, reciprocal obligation between humans and the land, and decision-making structures that were ecological before that word existed as a political category — are not only historically significant but practically relevant to the construction of post-capitalist societies. This is not romanticism but political ecology: Kadalie is interested in the institutional forms that sustained these relationships and in what those forms might mean for contemporary organising.

The connections Kadalie draws between Pan-Africanism and social ecology are not forced. Bookchin's libertarian municipalism — his argument for face-to-face democratic assemblies at the neighbourhood level as the organisational form of ecological politics — has structural parallels with the communal governance forms documented in African political anthropology. Kadalie is interested in these convergences without claiming they are identical, and without flattening the differences between African communities, between historical periods, or between theory and practice.

The book is also a contribution to the ongoing conversation about what Pan-Africanism means when it is not state-centred nationalism. Kadalie is explicit that the Pan-Africanism he is interested in is not the Pan-Africanism of African heads of state meeting in Addis Ababa but the Pan-Africanism of grassroots movements across the continent and diaspora building alternative institutions. This distinguishes his work from much of the Pan-Africanist canon and makes it genuinely useful for contemporary organising.

books.title: Anarchism and the Black Revolution
books.author: Lorenzo Kom'boa Ervin
books.summary: The 2021 expanded edition of Ervin's foundational pamphlet — with new afterword and analysis of contemporary movements.
books.body:
Lorenzo Kom'boa Ervin wrote the first version of Anarchism and the Black Revolution in 1979 while serving a life sentence in a United States federal prison. He had been convicted in 1969 of hijacking a plane to Cuba — a political act connected to his work with the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and, later, resistance to FBI counterintelligence operations against Black liberation movements. He was classified as a political prisoner. The pamphlet was initially circulated in photocopied form through prison networks and anarchist distribution channels.

The book's central argument is that Black liberation in America requires anarchism — not Black capitalism, which simply recycles exploitation under Black management, and not Black Marxist-Leninism, which reproduces the vanguard party structure and its tendency toward authoritarianism. Ervin was formed by his experience with SNCC's grassroots direct-action model and by his exposure to anarchist theory in prison, and he argues that the traditions converge: that the mutual aid networks, community self-defence organisations, and direct-action tactics of the Black freedom movement are in practice anarchist, whether they use that name or not.

Ervin is particularly sharp on the critique of nationalism. Black nationalism, he argues, mistakes the nation-state form — itself a product of European capitalism — for liberation. The goal is not a Black state but the destruction of the state form that has always served the ruling class. His analysis of the lumpenproletariat, the most marginalised section of the Black community that mainstream Marxism had written off as a potential revolutionary subject, draws on Fanon and anticipates much subsequent thinking about the political energy of those most excluded from formal institutions.

The pamphlet was expanded in 1993 and again in the Pluto Press edition of 2021, which includes a new foreword by Ervin reflecting on the Movement for Black Lives and contemporary conditions. Ervin was released from prison in 1983 after an international campaign and has continued organising in Chattanooga, Tennessee ever since. Anarchism and the Black Revolution is the most widely circulated Black anarchist text in English and one of the founding documents of the tradition this site is built to extend.
